newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria parlt dissolves, votes wider cabinet powers.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria parlt dissolves, votes wider cabinet powers.

text.p: Bulgaria's parliament disbanded on Thursday after approving a bill allowing an interim cabinet to conclude vital loan agreements with other governments or lending institutions before elections on April 19.
"Bulgaria is on the way to say 'good bye' to communism and a decisive 'yes' to market reform," opposition deputy Yudjel Atilla told the closing session.

Authorising the caretaker cabinet to negotiate with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) will pave the way for talks on new aid to accompany a strict fixed exchange rate regime to shore up a collapsing economy.

The interim cabinet, led by Sofia mayor Stefan Sofianski, inherits economic chaos from the outgoing socialist administration. Bulgaria has been without effective government since Zhan Videnov resigned as premier on December 21.
Missions are expected in the next few days from the European Union and the IMF, which suspended credits last year because the socialists failed to carry out promised reforms.

The outgoing parliament, wrapping up outstanding business, voted to lower the barrier for parties to enter parliament to three percent from four percent of the vote, paving the way for smaller parties to win seats.
It also voted amendments to the income tax law to take account of hyper-inflation and amendments to the state budget to allow stop-gap financing for agriculture.
President Petar Stoyanov appointed the caretaker cabinet on Wednesday, setting elections for April 19 and dissolving parliament with effect from February 19.
At its first session, the cabinet set up a Financial Stabilisation Council headed by Sofianski to implement financial stabilisation policy and negotiate with international lenders.

The caretaker cabinet plans to speed up long-delayed structural reforms such as privatisation and closing loss-making state firms, cut state spending, crack down on corruption and the grey economy and encourage investment.

After 30 days of mass protests fuelled by economic hardship, the socialist majority last week gave up efforts to form a new cabinet and agreed to elections 20 months before the end of their parliamentary term.
The IMF has said it is ready to send a mission to Sofia as soon as a new government is in place and Stoyanov has asked for aid to stabilise the economy before the introduction of a currency board.
The currency board mechanism would require levs in circulation to be matched by central bank reserves, severely limiting the powers of the government and the central bank.
